en: Sulfur sits under oxygen in the same group, so sulfur also has six valence electrons; the column, not the row, gives that number.
Fluorine sits one column right of oxygen, so fluorine has seven valence electrons, while oxygen in group 16 has six.
Nitrogen sits one column left of oxygen, so nitrogen has five valence electrons; stepping right to oxygen adds one, making six.
Carbon in group 14 has four valence electrons; oxygen is two groups farther right, so oxygen has six.
Oxygen heads the chalcogen family, group 16, whose members share six valence electrons even though their atoms get heavier down the column.
You do not have to list all eight electrons every time: oxygen's box on the table already tells you the outer count is six.
Oxygen is in the p-block with four p electrons plus two s electrons in the outer shell, totaling six valence electrons.
Valence electrons are the outer-shell electrons that do the bonding; for oxygen those outer electrons number six, from group 16.
Oxygen's two inner electrons are not valence electrons; only the six in the outer shell, shown by its group, count as valence.
When oxygen gains two electrons to fill its valence shell, it becomes O-two-minus, because six plus two makes eight.
In a water molecule oxygen makes two bonds, matching a need for two more electrons to finish a set of eight around six valence electrons.
On the table, find the symbol O, then look at the top of that column: the group label is how you name oxygen's six valence electrons.
Oxygen's period number is 2, which is not its valence count; the period is the shell, and the group gives the six valence electrons.
Selenium, farther down oxygen's column, still has six valence electrons; changing period does not change that group-16 outer count.
Tellurium is another group-16 element under oxygen, so it too has six valence electrons even though the atom is much heavier.
Oxygen is not a noble gas, so its outer shell is not full; six valence electrons leave two empty places in an octet.
A full outer shell for oxygen would be eight electrons; starting from six valence electrons, oxygen is two away from that octet.
Oxygen's box is on the right side of the table, in the p-block, where group 16 elements show six valence electrons.
Helium in group 18 has a full first shell of two, but oxygen's valence shell is the second shell with six electrons, not two.
In an oxygen molecule each atom still has six valence electrons; they share pairs so both can look like they have eight.
A double bond in O-two uses four shared electrons, which fits two oxygen atoms that each started with six valence electrons.
If a classmate says oxygen has eight valence electrons, check the group header: eight would be group 18, not oxygen's group 16.
The number you write for oxygen's valence electrons is six, not eight; eight is the atomic number, which counts all electrons.
When you draw oxygen, count the dots: if you drew eight dots you used neon's group, not oxygen's six valence electrons.
Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine share period 2 but not the same valence count: five, six, and seven as you move right.
Left-side metals often have one, two, or three valence electrons; oxygen on the right is a nonmetal with six.
Some textbooks title group 16 the oxygen family; that heading is a reminder that oxygen's valence electron number is six.
The outer configuration 2s-two 2p-four adds to six electrons, matching oxygen's group-16 place on the periodic table.
Knowing oxygen has six valence electrons from the table helps you predict it often needs two more electrons in compounds.
Oxygen has eight protons, but protons are not valence electrons; the table's group, not the proton count, gives the six outer electrons.
